## devonthink
CRITICAL — Database package safety: DEVONthink databases are stored as packages (.dtBase2) or sparse images (.dtSparse, .dtArchive). Never modify, rename, move, or delete files inside a database package directly via the filesystem. All record and content operations must go through this MCP server or, as a fallback, via AppleScript. Direct filesystem manipulation will corrupt the database and cause irreversible data loss.

Batch operations: Use the uuids array parameter instead of sequential single-record calls for tag, update, move, trash, duplicate, replicate, and export operations. Batch mode is faster, reduces round trips, and returns a summary with succeeded/failed counts.

Avoiding duplicates: Use lookup_records (by name, URL, path, filename, or comment) before create_record to check whether a record already exists.

Content editing: Prefer update_record_content with mode append or insert over replace for large documents. Replace mode requires sending the entire new content and risks accidental data loss if the content is incomplete.

Group hierarchies: Use create_group_path to create nested group structures in a single call (like mkdir -p) rather than sequential create_record calls.

AI-powered tools: classify_record and find_similar_records use DEVONthink's built-in AI algorithms and proprietary training data — they provide organizational suggestions that complement, not duplicate, your own capabilities.

Record enrichment: resolve_doi_metadata and resolve_book_metadata can enrich existing records with bibliographic metadata by passing the record's uuid — there is no need to create a new record.

AI exclusion: Records marked as excluded from AI access (excludeFromChat) are protected in two ways. (1) Input protection: any tool that receives such a record's UUID as an argument refuses to operate on it and returns an error. (2) Output protection: result lists from tools like search_records, classify_record, find_similar_records, get_record_children, get_record_duplicates, and the link traversal tools are filt… [truncated]

## omnifocus
OmniFocus is a GTD task manager. Hierarchy: Folders > Projects > Tasks > Subtasks.

TASK STATES: Available, Blocked, Deferred (future defer date), Flagged, Overdue, Completed, Dropped. Planned Date is a scheduling signal only — no availability/overdue constraints.

PROJECT TYPES: "sequential" (tasks in order; first incomplete = available, rest blocked; position = dependencies), "parallel" (all available), "single_actions" (no completion goal, cannot auto-complete). The `next` field is true for the first available action in a sequential project/action group; in parallel projects, all incomplete tasks have `next: true`.

ACTION GROUPS: Task with subtasks. Parent shows `blocked: true` while subtasks are active — this is normal, not an error. Do not try to unblock it.

INHERITED STATUS: `completed`/`dropped` reflect the task's own state, not its container's. `effectivelyCompleted`/`effectivelyDropped` reflect the container's state — if true, the task's parent project or action group was completed/dropped. Task in completed project: `completed: false`, `effectivelyCompleted: true`, `available: false`. Use `available_only=True` for actionable tasks.

EFFECTIVE DATES: Dates returned by get_tasks are always effective (inherited). A task with no direct due date WILL show its project's due date in the dueDate field — this is correct behavior, not a bug. You cannot clear an inherited date at the task level. Write operations set the task's own date.

RECURRING TASKS: `completed=True` uses `mark complete`, which creates the next occurrence. This is guaranteed. WARNING: Dropping a recurring task (status='dropped') without clearing recurrence first (recurrence='') spawns the next occurrence. To stop a series: update_tasks([{"id": "...", "recurrence": "", "status": "dropped"}]).

TAGS: Represent work contexts. Tag statuses: Active (normal), On Hold (tasks excluded from Available perspective), Dropped (tag hidden from picker; does NOT affect task availability).

DEFER vs DUE: Defer = hidden until that date. Due = deadline.

- code-review: Review the changes since a fixed point (commit, branch, tag, or merge-base) along two axes — Standards (does the code follow this repo's documented coding standards?) and Spec (does the code match what the originating issue/spec asked for?). Runs both reviews in parallel sub-agents and reports them side by side. Use when the user wants to review a branch, a PR, work-in-progress changes, or asks to "review since X".
- resolving-merge-conflicts: Use when you need to resolve an in-progress git merge/rebase conflict.
- seo-optimizer: Optimize content for search engines with keyword analysis, readability scoring, meta descriptions, and competitor comparison. Use this when users want to improve SEO, optimize blog posts, or analyze content for search performance.
- systems-thinking: Analyze problems using a Systems Thinking approach. Use when users mention "systems thinking," "systemic," "feedback loops," "unintended consequences," "root cause," "interconnected," or request analysis of complex, multi-factor problems. Guides conversation through questions and observations rather than prescriptive solutions.
- wizard: Generate an interactive bash wizard that walks a human through steps only they can perform. Use when provisioning infrastructure, setting up credentials or CI secrets, walking an unfamiliar third-party dashboard, or running a one-off migration or cutover. Don't invoke this for steps the agent can perform itself.
- writing-for-agents: Writing documents for agents. Use when creating or editing skills, or modifying AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md.
- add-backlinks: Add backlinks from related blog posts and glossary entries to a target post. Use when the user wants to improve internal linking by having other content link back to a specific article.
- blog-post: Create or revise a blog post for the Agile Pain Relief website. Use when the user wants to write a new blog post, revise/refresh an existing one, or update content. Guides through gathering information, content structure, internal linking, and post-publish steps.
- evergreen-posting: Compile Mark's selected social drafts into the batch JSON the posting pipeline consumes (LinkedIn / Mastodon / Bluesky), validating character limits and URL budgets, threading the link when it won't fit, and marking the source calendars so nothing is promoted twice. Blog/glossary/newsletter prose is authored and selected UPSTREAM as Markdown via the vault linkedin-style draft skill; this skill condenses the selected options to three platforms and writes the JSON, it does not re-draft that prose. Quiz posts are still drafted here from seeds. Use when Mark says "build the batch JSON", "compile the selected drafts", "schedule social media", or asks for the evergreen batch.
- glossary-entry: Create a new glossary term for the Agile Pain Relief website. Use when the user wants to add a new Agile/Scrum term definition, concept explanation, or methodology entry to the glossary.
- indexing-strategy: Use this skill when Mark asks to analyze, plan, or implement SEO topic clusters and internal linking for agilepainrelief.com. Covers two modes: (1) ANALYZE mode — audit existing content, identify pillar/cluster opportunities, find gaps and orphaned pages, and produce a prioritized action plan; (2) IMPLEMENT mode — generate specific internal linking instructions, write or revise blog posts and glossary entries to fit the cluster strategy, and produce per-page checklists. Also use when Mark asks what a blog post or glossary entry needs for SEO, or when he wants to check whether a draft meets the cluster linking requirements.
- newsletter: Draft and send a newsletter to the Newsletter Subscribers list via Cakemail, starting from plain markdown. Use when Mark wants to write, render, test, or dispatch a newsletter / email campaign, or turn a markdown file into a Cakemail draft campaign. Drives the email-automation CLI's send-newsletter command.
- social-media-adapt: Adapt LinkedIn posts to Mastodon and Bluesky formats with platform-specific character limits, thread formatting, and JSON structure. Use when Claude needs to convert LinkedIn content to other social platforms, create threaded posts, or adapt content for different character limits (see the shared conventions for current limits).
- claude-md-management:revise-claude-md: Update CLAUDE.md with learnings from this session
- claude-md-management:claude-md-improver: Audit and improve CLAUDE.md files in repositories. Use when user asks to check, audit, update, improve, or fix CLAUDE.md files. Scans for all CLAUDE.md files, evaluates quality against templates, outputs quality report, then makes targeted updates. Also use when the user mentions "CLAUDE.md maintenance" or "project memory optimization".
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.

First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

title: 'Which parts of the Scrum Master job still need a person?'

mapMove:
  reclaimPriority: ['q3', 'q1', 'q2']
  redirectPriority: ['q2', 'q4', 'q7', 'q8', 'q5', 'q6']

  # No band headline and no tier title: the shape carries the result, and it
  # deliberately shows proportions rather than a score.
  eyebrow: 'your result'
  heading: 'Here’s what I see'

  opening: |
    Just observations, and what I’d recommend you consider. Nobody finishes this doing all the right things.

  shape:
    label: 'Where your recent Sprints went'
    axisTop: 'needs a person'
    axisBottom: 'the tools are starting to do this'
    axisNear: 'one person'
    axisFar: 'wider than the team'
    tagFrom: 'less of this'
    tagTo: 'more of this'
    mostLine: 'Most of your last few Sprints went to {box}.'
    mostlyTop: 'Most of your time is already in work that needs a person.'
    mostlyBottom: 'Most of your time is in work the tools are starting to do.'
    boxes:
      - id: people
        name: 'the people work'
        row: top
        tone: valuable
      - id: system
        name: 'the system work'
        row: top
        tone: valuable
      - id: mechanical
        name: 'the mechanical work'
        row: bottom
        tone: slipping

  gainingHeading: 'getting more valuable'
  gainingEmpty: 'Not much showed up here this time, and that’s the point of the map, not a verdict on you.'

  slippingHeading: 'tools are starting to do this work'
  slippingEmpty: 'Nothing here. That’s rare, and it’s a good place to be. Keep doing what you’ve already started'

  contextHeading: 'about your situation'

  moveHeading: 'where I’d start'

  wellPositioned: |
    You’re the rare case. Most of your time is already in the work that’s getting more valuable: growing people, coaching the Product Owner, working the wider system around the team. There’s no admin pile to dig out of.

    Go deeper and help others do the same. The Scrum Masters who will thrive in the future aren’t just doing this work, they’re pulling their teams and peers along with them.

  # Shown when nothing was decisive enough to point at, which happens two ways:
  # every answer landed in the middle, or the only things that stood out were
  # constraints outside the taker's control. The copy has to cover both.
  noMove: |
    Nothing you said stands out enough for me to point at. Either your answers landed in the middle, or the things that did stand out are outside your control. Start with whichever question was hardest to answer.

  close: |
    There is no magic. GenAI will not magically you or your team more productive. Nor will it replace you. The ground under all of us is shifting, and the people who focus on the bigger picture of coaching their team and organization are the ones who will succeed.

  # The course is due to be renamed. `buttonLabel` is deliberately generic so
  # only `buttonHref` needs updating when the slug changes (and add a redirect
  # in src/constants/redirects.ts at that point).
  cta:
    body: 'Want to go deeper on the coaching side?'
    buttonLabel: 'See the course'
    buttonHref: '/surviving-the-ai-tsunami-an-evidenced-based-course/'

# Project History

A short, human-readable log of notable changes and the reasoning behind them.
Newest first. (Detailed, current behaviour lives in `CLAUDE.md`; this file is the
"why we did it" story.)

## 2026-08-04 — Course dates come from Corsizio, not from four hand-typed copies

**Why.** Course dates lived in four places: the `workshops` array in each course
page's frontmatter, `email-automation/newsletters/courses.json` for the
newsletter, the `date` in each `email-automation/courses/*.json` cohort config,
and the AI Tsunami page's prose. Three of the four were wrong on the day this was
written. The CSPO and CSD-technical pages were still advertising June classes
that had already run. `csm-virtual.json` said June 15 while the site sold
September 3. And `newsletters/courses.json` listed a July 28 CSM whose Corsizio
event returned 404 in every status: the course was cancelled after the newsletter
went out, so subscribers were sent a dead "Register" link. Nothing was broken in
a way anything would report; four copies of a fact simply drift.

**What it is now.** Corsizio is the source of truth. `npm run sync-courses`
writes `shared/course-schedule.json`, and the course pages, the "Get Certified"
tabs, the JSON-LD and the newsletter all read it. The cohort configs keep only
what Corsizio has never heard of (Zoom, Mural, docs folders) plus a
`corsizioEventId`; their dates resolve live. So it is two and a half places
collapsed into one, the half being the cohort config, which had to keep its own
file because no calendar system knows our Mural board.

**Why the file is committed rather than fetched at build.** A build-time fetch
would let a Corsizio outage break a deploy, and would *still* need scheduled
builds to notice a newly-scheduled course, so it buys fragility without escaping
staleness. Committed in `shared/`, pushing it triggers the rebuild by itself and
git records every schedule change.

**Why the email path fetches live anyway.** The generated file holds only future
events, but the post-course email is sent *after* the class, when the cohort's
event is no longer in it. So `resolveCourseConfig()` does a by-id lookup, which
Corsizio answers for past events. Two mechanisms, because they answer different
questions: "what is on sale" versus "what was this cohort". A deleted event 404s
and throws rather than falling back to a stale local date, so the cancelled-course
case that produced the dead newsletter link now stops a send instead.

**Mapping is by category id, not event name.** Every Corsizio event carries
exactly one category and the ids are stable, so retitling a workshop cannot break
the mapping; matching on names would have. Two things fell out of the probe worth
recording: `startDate`/`endDate` are UTC instants with a separate `timeZone`, so
every label and day count is computed in the event's zone or a 9am Toronto class
can round onto the wrong day; and multi-day courses are one event spanning first
start to last end, which is what makes `numberOfDays` and the daily window
derivable at all. That holds only because none of our courses use Corsizio's
`breakdownDates` for per-session hours.

**A wrong price was being published to Google.** `structured-data.astro` had a
hardcoded price table listing CSD at 1195 when we charge 995/1095, and it
regex-parsed the free-text frontmatter date, falling back to *today* whenever the
pattern missed, which published permanently-current events. Both are gone: real
ISO dates, and real prices as an `AggregateOffer` when personal and regular
registration differ. Courses with nothing scheduled now emit no Event markup at
all, which is correct, and their "None currently scheduled" button is rendered
from an empty list rather than being a placeholder row someone had to remember to
type.

## 2026-08-04 — Quiz results: a shape instead of a balance bar, and the move stops going silent

**Why.** The `map-move` results page led with a two-segment balance bar: the
proportion of gaining to slipping answers. It could say "this much of your time
was well spent" and nothing else, so it could not answer the question the page
exists to answer, which is why one area deserves attention ahead of another.

A radar chart was the first idea and was wrong, for a reason worth writing down:
**a radar needs a number on every axis, and this quiz deliberately has none.**
Answers are classified, not scored. Drawing one would have meant inventing the
numbers and then presenting them as measurement, and a `context` answer ("there
is no Product Owner I can coach") would have plotted as a low point, reading as
the taker's failing when the whole design says it is not.

**What replaced it.** A fixed grid of named kinds of work, each carrying a bar
showing how much of the taker's time went to it. Two new per-option fields feed
it, `box` and `weight`, both independent of `bucket`: the bucket says
strength-or-gap, the box says what kind of work, and those are genuinely
orthogonal ("almost no time on coaching" is a slipping answer about an
appreciating box). There is still no number on the page.

**The mosaic that lost, and why it matters.** The first build drew each box at
the actual size of its share, which is a better picture of where the time went
and was the version everyone preferred on sight. It failed on the case the page
exists for. The box being recommended is by definition the one the taker has
given least time to, so it was always the smallest box on the picture and always
the first too small to hold its own label. Label thresholds, a fallback key
below the picture, and finally the move tag migrating into that key were all
machinery to paper over a picture arguing against its own recommendation. Fixed
boxes plus a bar say the same thing about proportion and guarantee every box can
be read. Worth knowing before anyone rebuilds the mosaic.

**Three more things fell out of building it, each worth keeping.**

_A quadrant needed a fourth box that could not exist._ Splitting the bottom row
by scope (one person versus wider than the team) produced "your own overhead",
which exactly one option in thirty-two could reach, and only if the taker was
part-time. For a full-timer the box was not rare, it was unreachable. Adding a
ninth question to fill it made things worse, not better: it converted an empty
box into an unlabellable sliver and pushed label eviction from 17% to 34%. The
fix was to stop splitting the row. Every automatable thing a Scrum Master does is
mechanical, whether it is a ticket, a status round-up or a set of slides.

_The arrow had to go._ A curve from the box to take time from to the box to put
it into was hard to follow and made the picture busy. Two accent words on the two
boxes say the same thing and nothing crosses the picture.

**The bug this uncovered.** `eligible()` in `map-move.ts` accepted any `slipping`
answer for a half of the move whether or not a sentence existed for that half.
`q2`'s "status and logistics desk" sits first in `redirectPriority` and has a
`reclaimSentence` but no `redirectSentence`, so on **16% of all answer sets** it
won the redirect and then rendered nothing: the taker was told what to stop doing
and never told where the time should go. Worse, once the shape existed it also
put "more of this" on the mechanical work, which is advice to spend more time on
the coordination machine. Requiring the sentence (already the rule for `context`
answers) makes the walk carry on to the next candidate that has something to say.

Measured over all 65,536 answer sets, complete moves went from 52.0% to 65.9%,
and a new `reclaimSentence` on `q1`'s part-time answer took it to 74.7%. Nothing

content.content:
123	## 2026-07-30 — Quiz copy pass: all eight questions, one at a time
124	
125	**Why.** The questions had accumulated three tics. Half of them opened "Think
126	about" or "Think back"; "the last couple of Sprints" appeared in three questions
127	plus the intro, the how-it-works strip, the section blurb, `heroBody` and
128	`description`, so a taker met it three times before question 1; and several
129	middles were hedges rather than answers, the worst being q5's bare "A bit of
130	both". With `randomizeOptions: 'shuffle'` on, an answer that points at its
131	neighbours points at whatever the shuffle put there, so every option has to read
132	cold with no siblings in view. Mark reviewed each question in turn and rewrote in
133	his own voice where the suggestion missed it.
134	
135	**Two rules came out of the pass and are worth keeping.**
136	
137	_Result sentences must stand alone._ The results page renders map, reclaim and
138	redirect sentences only; it uses the question object solely to look up an icon
139	(`MapMoveResults.astro`), so the question text and the answer text are never on
140	screen with them. Trimming a result sentence because it "repeats the question" is
141	therefore always wrong, and it cost q8's map line the list defining what "craft"
142	means before Mark caught it. De-duplicating a map line against its _own_ reclaim
143	line is still right: those two do render together.
144	
145	_Question and answer text are the opposite case._ They are read with the question
146	in view, so a phrase repeated from the question stem is dead weight there.
147	
148	**Two factual errors, not style.** q3's part-time answer claimed a part-time
149	Scrum Master has less admin. The load comes from the team existing, so it is the
150	same either way and lands in fewer hours, which makes it worse. And q6's slipping
151	map said the impediment "sat there or got worked around" when working around it
152	is a _different answer_ in the same question, so it told people they had done
153	something they hadn't.
154	
155	**Two outright bugs:** q7's map had a stray comma between subject and verb plus a
156	dropped "of the" ("is one earliest and most important activities"), and q4's
157	redirect sentence had no full stop.
158	
159	**Vocabulary.** Mark never says "blocker", always "impediment". That word had
160	leaked into two questions, two answers and an icon name; the icon rename reached
161	`QuizIcon.tsx` and the engine README. "Sprint" is capitalised throughout, in the
162	quiz and in the CTA copy that quotes it. `PO` is spelled out everywhere, because
163	shuffled options mean there is no stable first use to define an abbreviation
164	against.
165	
166	**One priority change with real effect.** `redirectPriority` now leads with `q2`.
167	If nobody brings the Scrum Master anything, finding out why sits upstream of
168	every coaching gap below it: you cannot coach people who do not come to you, so
169	"put the time into coaching" is not yet actionable advice for that person.
170	
171	**Two more engine features fell out of it.** A `context` answer can now win the
172	**reclaim**, not just the redirect, on the same opt-in: supply that half's
173	sentence or stay in the context strip. The part-timer drowning in admin is
174	exactly who most needs "reclaim the admin time" and could never be given it,
175	because reclaim was slipping-only. `wellPositioned` had to learn about it too, or
176	it renders instead of the move and swallows the result. And `label` on a question
177	supplies the eyebrow text where there is no section to supply it.
178	
179	**Comments came out.** Mark almost never writes them, and every comment in the
180	repo was generated rather than authored; a needed comment usually means the work
181	is badly framed. The five added to the quiz frontmatter during this work were
182	removed, which is why the reasoning above lives here instead.
183	
184	## 2026-07-30 — Quiz asks the taker's role first: `profile` questions, `tag`, `lens`
185	
186	**Why.** The quiz reads as a Scrum Master's quiz, but the people taking it also
187	include part-time Scrum Masters, project managers running the process, and
188	managers of Scrum Masters. Knowing which one is in front of us is worth having
189	in Cakemail for segmentation, and for a manager it changes what the questions
190	even mean.
191	
192	**Plain "Team Member" was deliberately dropped.** It was on the original list
193	and it was the one persona that genuinely broke the quiz: q7 (coaching the
194	Product Owner) and q8 (the team's craft) would have scored a team member's
195	_correct_ answers as gaps, and q7 sits second in `redirectPriority`, so that
196	misread would frequently have become the single recommendation they walked away
197	with. The role list is now Scrum Master / part-time Scrum Master / project
198	manager / manager, all of whom do the work the questions ask about.
199	
200	**Three engine features, not a one-off.** The quiz engine is meant to be
201	extractable, so this went in as general capability:
202	
203	- `kind: 'profile'` on a question. It classifies the taker rather than assessing
204	  them: no score, no map entry, no progress bar, and it always leads regardless
205	  of `randomize`. Excluding it from progress is what keeps the cover's promise of
206	  "eight questions" true without recounting, and excluding it from the map is
207	  what stops "I'm a project manager" appearing as a line in the context strip
208	  and skewing the balance bar.
209	- `tag` on an option, applied to the submission as `tags[<name>]=true` alongside
210	  the static `submissionTags`. This is what carries the role to Cakemail. Note it
211	  needs answers to exist at submit time, so like `levelTagPrefix` it collects
212	  nothing on a start gate.
213	- `lens` on an option: a standing instruction shown from the moment that answer
214	  is picked and repeated above every later question. Every question in this quiz
215	  says "you", so a manager would otherwise answer about their own week and get a
216	  map of the wrong job. The repeat is the point: a one-off note at question 0 is
217	  forgotten by question 3.
218	
219	**Also fixed a latent bug next door.** `MapMoveResults.astro` rendered a context
220	answer with no `mapSentence` as a bare icon beside an empty line, and would have
221	rendered the panel as a heading over an empty list. Profile questions no longer
222	reach it, but the guard is right anyway.
223	
224	**The copy pass that followed** is the entry above this one.
225	
226	## 2026-07-30 — Quiz headline rewritten, and the sidebar CTA moved into `cta.ts`
227	
228	**Why.** "Where is the Scrum Master role going in an AI world?" was a third-person
229	industry question. The quiz doesn't answer that; it answers "which parts of _your_
230	last two sprints are gaining value and which are slipping". A headline that poses
231	an essay question invites the reader to go find someone's blog post about it. The
232	new one, "Which parts of the Scrum Master job still need a person?", promises the
233	personal readout the quiz actually delivers, and reads two ways on purpose: the
234	Scrum Master hears "what makes me valuable", a manager hears "what am I staffing
235	for".
236	
237	**The audience question, left open here and closed the same day.** Mark wanted a
238	manager who isn't a Scrum Master to see themselves here. All eight questions are
239	first-person and about work you personally did ("came to _you_", "_your_ time",
240	"what did _you_ actually do"), so the split isn't by job title. A Project Manager
241	or part-time Scrum Master who runs the events and chases status answers all eight
242	honestly and gets a useful map; only the label was keeping them out, which the
243	widened `heroBody` fixes. For a manager, q1 is the question that breaks (their
244	hours go to 1:1s, hiring and escalation, and no option fits); q4, q5 and q6
245	travel to them unchanged. The fix landed later the same day as the `lens` on the
246	role question, above: tell the manager to answer for their Scrum Master, and keep
247	telling them.
248	
249	**Three surfaces, three registers.** The banner and the blog/glossary sidebar
250	carry the landing page's headline verbatim, because both are read at browsing
251	pace and exact message match beats brevity. The modal fires 30 seconds into a
252	post and gets about two seconds of attention, so it drops the job title and goes
253	second person. The shared phrase "still need a person" is what keeps all three
254	matched to the landing page.
255	
256	**`link-sidebar.astro` no longer owns copy.** It had its own hardcoded heading,
257	body, link text, image and alt as prop defaults, which is how it came to be
258	advertising the old headline after the quiz had moved on. Both callers render
259	`<LinkSidebar />` bare, so the props were dead flexibility hiding a drift hazard.
260	Copy now comes from `CTA_PRIMARY` (new `sidebarBody` / `sidebarButtonText`
261	fields) and imagery from a new `SIDEBAR_IMAGES`, matching how `cta-banner.astro`
262	and `modal-popup.astro` already read the constants. `src/constants/cta.ts` is now
263	the only file to edit for CTA copy on all three surfaces.
264	
265	## 2026-07-30 — Quiz email capture moved back to the end, with the ask stated on the cover
266	
267	**Why.** The hard gate worked (signups arrive, Turnstile holds), but asking for
268	an email before question 1 charges the visitor before they've seen anything.
269	Someone who has answered eight questions has already invested; someone who has
270	read a cover has not. Moving the ask back to the end trades a self-qualified,
271	smaller list for a larger one, and the reflective `map-move` result is the kind
272	of thing people want _after_ the thinking, not a prize they bid on up front.
273	
274	**What we did.** `scrum-master-ai` frontmatter went back to
275	`capturePosition: 'end'`. The engine already supported both positions, so no
276	engine code changed: the stepper puts the "Before you start" card back as step 0
277	under the cover, the hero's own "Start the quiz" button returns, and the capture
278	card (first name optional + email) becomes the last step. `captureButtonLabel`

## 2026-07-30 — Quiz copy pass: all eight questions, one at a time

**Why.** The questions had accumulated three tics. Half of them opened "Think
about" or "Think back"; "the last couple of Sprints" appeared in three questions
plus the intro, the how-it-works strip, the section blurb, `heroBody` and
`description`, so a taker met it three times before question 1; and several
middles were hedges rather than answers, the worst being q5's bare "A bit of
both". With `randomizeOptions: 'shuffle'` on, an answer that points at its
neighbours points at whatever the shuffle put there, so every option has to read
cold with no siblings in view. Mark reviewed each question in turn and rewrote in
his own voice where the suggestion missed it.

**Two rules came out of the pass and are worth keeping.**

_Result sentences must stand alone._ The results page renders map, reclaim and
redirect sentences only; it uses the question object solely to look up an icon
(`MapMoveResults.astro`), so the question text and the answer text are never on
screen with them. Trimming a result sentence because it "repeats the question" is
therefore always wrong, and it cost q8's map line the list defining what "craft"
means before Mark caught it. De-duplicating a map line against its _own_ reclaim
line is still right: those two do render together.

_Question and answer text are the opposite case._ They are read with the question
in view, so a phrase repeated from the question stem is dead weight there.

**Two factual errors, not style.** q3's part-time answer claimed a part-time
Scrum Master has less admin. The load comes from the team existing, so it is the
same either way and lands in fewer hours, which makes it worse. And q6's slipping
map said the impediment "sat there or got worked around" when working around it
is a _different answer_ in the same question, so it told people they had done
something they hadn't.

**Two outright bugs:** q7's map had a stray comma between subject and verb plus a
dropped "of the" ("is one earliest and most important activities"), and q4's
redirect sentence had no full stop.

**Vocabulary.** Mark never says "blocker", always "impediment". That word had
leaked into two questions, two answers and an icon name; the icon rename reached
`QuizIcon.tsx` and the engine README. "Sprint" is capitalised throughout, in the
quiz and in the CTA copy that quotes it. `PO` is spelled out everywhere, because
shuffled options mean there is no stable first use to define an abbreviation
against.

**One priority change with real effect.** `redirectPriority` now leads with `q2`.
If nobody brings the Scrum Master anything, finding out why sits upstream of
every coaching gap below it: you cannot coach people who do not come to you, so
"put the time into coaching" is not yet actionable advice for that person.

**Two more engine features fell out of it.** A `context` answer can now win the
**reclaim**, not just the redirect, on the same opt-in: supply that half's
sentence or stay in the context strip. The part-timer drowning in admin is
exactly who most needs "reclaim the admin time" and could never be given it,
because reclaim was slipping-only. `wellPositioned` had to learn about it too, or
it renders instead of the move and swallows the result. And `label` on a question
supplies the eyebrow text where there is no section to supply it.

**Comments came out.** Mark almost never writes them, and every comment in the
repo was generated rather than authored; a needed comment usually means the work
is badly framed. The five added to the quiz frontmatter during this work were
removed, which is why the reasoning above lives here instead.

## 2026-07-30 — Quiz asks the taker's role first: `profile` questions, `tag`, `lens`

**Why.** The quiz reads as a Scrum Master's quiz, but the people taking it also
include part-time Scrum Masters, project managers running the process, and
managers of Scrum Masters. Knowing which one is in front of us is worth having
in Cakemail for segmentation, and for a manager it changes what the questions
even mean.

**Plain "Team Member" was deliberately dropped.** It was on the original list
and it was the one persona that genuinely broke the quiz: q7 (coaching the
Product Owner) and q8 (the team's craft) would have scored a team member's
_correct_ answers as gaps, and q7 sits second in `redirectPriority`, so that
misread would frequently have become the single recommendation they walked away
with. The role list is now Scrum Master / part-time Scrum Master / project
manager / manager, all of whom do the work the questions ask about.

**Three engine features, not a one-off.** The quiz engine is meant to be
extractable, so this went in as general capability:

- `kind: 'profile'` on a question. It classifies the taker rather than assessing
  them: no score, no map entry, no progress bar, and it always leads regardless
  of `randomize`. Excluding it from progress is what keeps the cover's promise of
  "eight questions" true without recounting, and excluding it from the map is
  what stops "I'm a project manager" appearing as a line in the context strip
  and skewing the balance bar.
- `tag` on an option, applied to the submission as `tags[<name>]=true` alongside
  the static `submissionTags`. This is what carries the role to Cakemail. Note it
  needs answers to exist at submit time, so like `levelTagPrefix` it collects
  nothing on a start gate.
- `lens` on an option: a standing instruction shown from the moment that answer
  is picked and repeated above every later question. Every question in this quiz
  says "you", so a manager would otherwise answer about their own week and get a
  map of the wrong job. The repeat is the point: a one-off note at question 0 is
  forgotten by question 3.

**Also fixed a latent bug next door.** `MapMoveResults.astro` rendered a context
answer with no `mapSentence` as a bare icon beside an empty line, and would have
rendered the panel as a heading over an empty list. Profile questions no longer
reach it, but the guard is right anyway.

**The copy pass that followed** is the entry above this one.

## 2026-07-30 — Quiz headline rewritten, and the sidebar CTA moved into `cta.ts`

**Why.** "Where is the Scrum Master role going in an AI world?" was a third-person
industry question. The quiz doesn't answer that; it answers "which parts of _your_
last two sprints are gaining value and which are slipping". A headline that poses
an essay question invites the reader to go find someone's blog post about it. The
new one, "Which parts of the Scrum Master job still need a person?", promises the
personal readout the quiz actually delivers, and reads two ways on purpose: the
Scrum Master hears "what makes me valuable", a manager hears "what am I staffing
for".

**The audience question, left open here and closed the same day.** Mark wanted a
manager who isn't a Scrum Master to see themselves here. All eight questions are
first-person and about work you personally did ("came to _you_", "_your_ time",
"what did _you_ actually do"), so the split isn't by job title. A Project Manager
or part-time Scrum Master who runs the events and chases status answers all eight
honestly and gets a useful map; only the label was keeping them out, which the
widened `heroBody` fixes. For a manager, q1 is the question that breaks (their
hours go to 1:1s, hiring and escalation, and no option fits); q4, q5 and q6
travel to them unchanged. The fix landed later the same day as the `lens` on the
role question, above: tell the manager to answer for their Scrum Master, and keep
telling them.

**Three surfaces, three registers.** The banner and the blog/glossary sidebar
carry the landing page's headline verbatim, because both are read at browsing
pace and exact message match beats brevity. The modal fires 30 seconds into a
post and gets about two seconds of attention, so it drops the job title and goes
second person. The shared phrase "still need a person" is what keeps all three
matched to the landing page.

**`link-sidebar.astro` no longer owns copy.** It had its own hardcoded heading,
body, link text, image and alt as prop defaults, which is how it came to be
advertising the old headline after the quiz had moved on. Both callers render
`<LinkSidebar />` bare, so the props were dead flexibility hiding a drift hazard.
Copy now comes from `CTA_PRIMARY` (new `sidebarBody` / `sidebarButtonText`
fields) and imagery from a new `SIDEBAR_IMAGES`, matching how `cta-banner.astro`
and `modal-popup.astro` already read the constants. `src/constants/cta.ts` is now
the only file to edit for CTA copy on all three surfaces.

## 2026-07-30 — Quiz email capture moved back to the end, with the ask stated on the cover

**Why.** The hard gate worked (signups arrive, Turnstile holds), but asking for
an email before question 1 charges the visitor before they've seen anything.
Someone who has answered eight questions has already invested; someone who has
read a cover has not. Moving the ask back to the end trades a self-qualified,
smaller list for a larger one, and the reflective `map-move` result is the kind
of thing people want _after_ the thinking, not a prize they bid on up front.

**What we did.** `scrum-master-ai` frontmatter went back to
`capturePosition: 'end'`. The engine already supported both positions, so no
engine code changed: the stepper puts the "Before you start" card back as step 0
under the cover, the hero's own "Start the quiz" button returns, and the capture
card (first name optional + email) becomes the last step. `captureButtonLabel`
was dropped so the capture button falls back to `submitButtonLabel`, "Show me my
map", which is now literally what it does; `captureBody` was added because the
end capture renders a paragraph the compact gate had no room for.

**The cover still says the email is coming.** That was the one thing worth
keeping from the gate: nobody should meet the form as a surprise. `heroButtonNote`
under the start button and the closing line of `intro` both say the email is
asked for after the last question, before the map. The `heroButtonNote` field
exists for exactly this (it was added so the hero could never promise "at the
end" on a start-gated quiz) and it now earns its keep in the other direction.

**Then the cover had to be rebalanced.** Restoring the end capture put the
"Before you start" card back into the stepper with its own button, so it went
from a short static block wedged mid-page to a tall centred island terminating
an otherwise left-aligned page. `QuizIntroCard` is now left-aligned like every
other block. The centring had been deliberate, and the component's comment
explained the reasoning correctly (centred lines get hard to track past ~46
characters), but it constrained the _measure_ and not the _length_: once the
copy grew to two paragraphs plus a button, centring stopped reading as a pause
and started reading as a different design language.

**The email note was set as small print, which was backwards.** A quiz that
sells itself on candour cannot whisper the one thing it asks for. It moved from
muted `text-sm` to `text-base` italic in `ink-secondary`, held to the hero
body's measure so it reads as part of the pitch rather than a disclaimer under
the button.

**One measure down the whole cover.** The hero paragraphs were capped at 52ch
while `QuizIntroCard` ran to 60ch, so the reading column narrowed and then
widened again on the way down the page, which is the sort of thing you feel
before you see. Everything on the cover is 60ch now. The card's text is still
inset by the card's own padding, so the left edges don't align and shouldn't:
it's the same measure, not the same margin.

Transcript extracted to `temp/quiz-feedback-excerpt.txt` (gitignored). Comparing Mike's + Christopher's feedback against the quiz as it stands today:

## Already done since July 29

- **Email capture back at the end**, with the ask stated on the cover (`heroButtonNote` + `intro`) — commit `eba5abc2`
- **Profile question first** ("which role best describes you") with `role-*` tags and a manager `lens` — commit `6c59dfda`
- **"A bit of both" hedge answers** rewritten so every option reads cold and refers to the question
- **Old q4 (team vs wider system)** rewritten as a question first, answers second — Mike's exact prescription
- **Question copy pass** over all eight (tics, repetition, two factual errors)
- **More value in the report** — the `MapMoveShape` visual (2026-08-04) directly answers "make the transaction feel worth the email"

## Not addressed

1. **"Get one thing to try"** — `index.mdx:34`. Mike: *"get rid of the word try… try is like, eh, maybe this will work, maybe it won't."* Suggested "one thing to focus on". Still says "try". One-word fix.
2. **`heading: 'Here's what I see'`** — `index.mdx:370`. Called out as too generic; it's the first thing on the results page and says nothing about *them*. (The shape's `mostLine` right below it now does say something specific, which softens this, but the headline itself is unchanged.)
3. **`contextHeading: 'about your situation'`** — `index.mdx:406`. Mike, verbatim: *"don't say generic 'about your situation'. Make it specific to their situation."* Unchanged.
4. **Role × result personalisation** — the biggest unaddressed item. Mike's plan was roles × buckets so the copy speaks to a part-time SM differently from a full-timer. Today the role tag only goes to Cakemail and drives the manager `lens`; **no results copy varies by role**.
5. **Pain-led headline** — Mike's bet: *"Are you a Scrum Master concerned about your role disappearing in the age of AI?… probably triple your conversion rate."* The headline was rewritten on July 30 to "Which parts of the Scrum Master job still need a person?" for good reasons (recorded in `HISTORY.md`), but that's a *different* direction, not this one. The fear-led framing has never been tried, and it's the item Mike weighted most heavily.

## Partially

- **Question length.** The copy pass fixed tone, not length. Still long: q5 (146 chars), q7 (190), q8 (140). Mike asked for two lines max on each.
- **Value buried at the bottom.** "Where I'd start" is still last. Mike said that's fine *if* everything above leads up to it. The shape's `less of this` / `more of this` tags now foreshadow it, but nothing else on the page points forward to it.

## Explicitly rejected (not an oversight)

- **Named archetype result titles** ("you're the fire hose"). `CLAUDE.md` records "no number, letter or tier title anywhere" as a hard requirement. Items 2 and 3 above are still fixable without reintroducing an archetype.
- **Christopher's separate-entry-links-per-role** idea — the profile question was chosen instead.

Unrelated, spotted while reading: `index.mdx:422` reads *"GenAI will not magically you or your team more productive"* — missing "make".

content.text:
Proposals below, each with the exact edit. Nothing applied yet.

---

## 1. "one thing to try" → "focus on"

`src/content/quizzes/scrum-master-ai/index.mdx:34`

```yaml
- title: 'Get one thing to try'
+ title: 'Get one thing to focus on'
```

Body underneath already says "The single change I'd make first", which is the non-tentative register Mike wanted. `moveHeading: 'where I'd start'` needs no change.

**Cost:** one word.

---

## 2. Results heading: make it say something specific

`index.mdx:370` `heading: 'Here's what I see'` is the H1 and says nothing about them. The shape's `mostLine` two blocks below *does* ("Most of your last few Sprints went to the mechanical work.") — it's specific, it names the work not the person, and it's exactly the agree-or-disagree-with-me sentence Christopher asked for. It's just in the wrong place.

**Proposal: promote it into the heading and delete the duplicate.**

```yaml
  heading: 'Most of your recent Sprints went to {box}'
  # mostLine: removed — the heading carries it now
```

`mostlyTop` / `mostlyBottom` stay as the reading line under the shape (they only print when they disagree with the largest box, so they still earn their place).

**Engine change:** interpolate `{box}` in `heading` in `MapMoveResults.astro` using `result.shape.largestBoxId`, same substitution `MapMoveShape.astro:99` already does. Falls back to the literal string when `result.shape` is null (every answer mixed), so add a plain `headingFallback: 'Here's what I see'`.

Alternatives if you'd rather the H1 not be a bar-chart caption:
- `'Your last few Sprints went mostly to {box}'`
- `'Where your Sprints actually went'` (specific to the *page*, not to them — weaker, but no engine change)

---

## 3. `contextHeading: 'about your situation'`

`index.mdx:406`. Mike quoted this one verbatim as the generic-language example.

Recommend: **`'the constraints you described'`**

Rejected alternatives: "what you're up against" (too combative for a strip that's meant to be soft), "your situation, specifically" (still says "situation").

**One wrinkle to decide:** seven of the eight context sentences are genuine constraints, but q8's ("coaching through the work as you go is a legitimate way to grow a team's craft… count it, don't discount it") is a *positive*, and it reads oddly under "constraints". Two ways out — give q8's context answer a `redirectSentence` so it leaves the strip, or accept the mismatch. I'd accept it; it's one option in thirty-two.

---

## 4. Role × result personalisation — the big one

Currently the role tag goes to Cakemail and drives the manager `lens`, and that's all. Nothing on the results page varies by who they are.

The hook already exists: `map-move.ts:33` notes profile answers stay in the `a=` query string *specifically* so the page can branch on them later.

**Proposal — role-conditional copy overrides on `mapMove`:**

```yaml
mapMove:
  roleVariants:
    profileQuestion: role
    variants:
      role-part-time-sm:
        opening: |
          You're doing this job in the hours left over from another one, so
          judge what follows by what you did with the time you had.
        close: |
          ...
      role-manager:
        opening: |
          This is a map of your Scrum Master's last few Sprints, not yours.
          ...
      role-project-manager:
        opening: |
          ...
```

Variant keys reuse the option's existing `tag` — one identifier per role, no new vocabulary. Fields shallow-override the base `mapMove`.

**Scope: only `opening`, `close` and `cta`.** Not the per-answer sentences, not the move, not the map columns — those are already specific to what they answered, which is the substance of what Mike was asking for. Mike's full version was roles × ~5 buckets, i.e. 15-20 copy blocks; with four roles that's a 4× maintenance multiplier on copy you maintain alone, for a page whose per-answer text is already personalised. Three variant `opening`s buy most of the "you're speaking to me" effect for a fraction of it. The `cta` override is the one with a direct revenue argument: a manager should not be sold the same course landing as a part-time Scrum Master.

**Engine change:** a `MapMoveRoleVariants` type + schema entry, and a merge in `MapMoveResults.astro` (find the profile question, read its answer's `tag`, spread the variant over `mm`). ~30 lines. Copy is the real work.

---

## 5. Pain-led headline

`HISTORY.md` (2026-07-30) records the current headline as a deliberate decision, and the reasoning holds — but it argues against the *third-person essay question*, not against Mike's *fear-led* framing, which has never been tried. Mike bet a tripled conversion rate on it.

**Proposal: keep the headline, add a kicker above it** — gets the pain lead without discarding the documented reasoning.

```yaml
heroKicker: 'For Scrum Masters wondering if the role survives this'
heroHeading: 'Which parts of the Scrum Master job still need a person?'
```

And close `heroBody` on Mike's second half ("not just eight quick questions — find out how future-proof your role really is"):

```yaml
heroBody: 'Eight quick questions about how you actually spent the last couple
  of Sprints. See which parts of the work are getting more valuable, and which
  parts the tools are starting to do. Works whether you hold the title, cover it
  alongside delivery work, or run the process as a project manager.'
```
→ append: `'You'll see how much of your week is already work a tool could take.'`

**Engine change:** new `heroKicker` field + schema + render above the `h1` in `src/pages/quiz/[slug].astro:85`.

content.content:
280	`bucket` says whether the answer is a strength or a gap; `box` says what kind of
281	work it is. They are genuinely orthogonal: "almost no time on coaching" is a
282	`slipping` answer about an *appreciating* box. `weight` sizes the shape and
283	nothing else. It is not a score, is never summed against a maximum, and never
284	appears on the page. Every answered option contributes whatever its bucket,
285	because the shape asks "where did the time go", not "what went well" — which is
286	the opposite of the two map columns beside it, deliberately.
287	
288	The layout is declared once:
289	
290	```yaml
291	mapMove:
292	  shape:
293	    label: 'Where your recent Sprints went'
294	    axisTop: 'needs a person'
295	    axisBottom: 'the tools are starting to do this'
296	    axisNear: 'one person' # optional ends of the horizontal axis
297	    axisFar: 'wider than the team'
298	    tagFrom: 'less of this' # two or three words, in place of an arrow
299	    tagTo: 'more of this'
300	    mostLine: 'Most of your last few Sprints went to {box}.'
301	    mostlyTop: 'Most of your time is already in work that needs a person.'
302	    mostlyBottom: 'Most of your time is in work the tools are starting to do.'
303	    boxes:
304	      - { id: people, name: 'the people work', row: top, tone: valuable }
305	      - { id: system, name: 'the system work', row: top, tone: valuable }
306	      - { id: mechanical, name: 'the mechanical work', row: bottom, tone: slipping }
307	```
308	
309	Three things about that are load-bearing.
310	
311	**Name the work, never the person.** "the people work", not "the Coach". The
312	archetype is the thing this style refuses to hand out, and a box label is the
313	easiest place to smuggle one back in.
314	
315	**A row may hold one box.** Putting a single box on a row says the horizontal
316	distinction does not exist down there. `scrum-master-ai` does that on the bottom
317	row: every automatable thing a Scrum Master does is mechanical whether it is a
318	ticket, a status round-up or a set of slides, and splitting the row by scope
319	produced a box only a part-timer could ever reach.
320	
321	**There is no arrow.** The move is marked by `tagFrom` / `tagTo` on the two boxes
322	involved. A curve across the picture was hard to follow and made the whole thing
323	busy. `mostLine` (with `{box}` replaced by the largest box's name) and the
324	top/bottom line carry the reading in prose underneath; the top/bottom line is
325	suppressed when the largest box already sits on the majority row, because there

file.content:
`bucket` says whether the answer is a strength or a gap; `box` says what kind of
work it is. They are genuinely orthogonal: "almost no time on coaching" is a
`slipping` answer about an *appreciating* box. `weight` sizes the shape and
nothing else. It is not a score, is never summed against a maximum, and never
appears on the page. Every answered option contributes whatever its bucket,
because the shape asks "where did the time go", not "what went well" — which is
the opposite of the two map columns beside it, deliberately.

The layout is declared once:

```yaml
mapMove:
  shape:
    label: 'Where your recent Sprints went'
    axisTop: 'needs a person'
    axisBottom: 'the tools are starting to do this'
    axisNear: 'one person' # optional ends of the horizontal axis
    axisFar: 'wider than the team'
    tagFrom: 'less of this' # two or three words, in place of an arrow
    tagTo: 'more of this'
    mostLine: 'Most of your last few Sprints went to {box}.'
    mostlyTop: 'Most of your time is already in work that needs a person.'
    mostlyBottom: 'Most of your time is in work the tools are starting to do.'
    boxes:
      - { id: people, name: 'the people work', row: top, tone: valuable }
      - { id: system, name: 'the system work', row: top, tone: valuable }
      - { id: mechanical, name: 'the mechanical work', row: bottom, tone: slipping }
```

Three things about that are load-bearing.

**Name the work, never the person.** "the people work", not "the Coach". The
archetype is the thing this style refuses to hand out, and a box label is the
easiest place to smuggle one back in.

**A row may hold one box.** Putting a single box on a row says the horizontal
distinction does not exist down there. `scrum-master-ai` does that on the bottom
row: every automatable thing a Scrum Master does is mechanical whether it is a
ticket, a status round-up or a set of slides, and splitting the row by scope
produced a box only a part-timer could ever reach.

**There is no arrow.** The move is marked by `tagFrom` / `tagTo` on the two boxes
involved. A curve across the picture was hard to follow and made the whole thing
busy. `mostLine` (with `{box}` replaced by the largest box's name) and the
top/bottom line carry the reading in prose underneath; the top/bottom line is
suppressed when the largest box already sits on the majority row, because there
it only restates the sentence before it.

Two implementation notes. The component is HTML rather than SVG on purpose: an
SVG's text scales with its viewBox, so a 15px label renders at about 8px on a
phone. And **bars are scaled by their row's box count**, because a row holding
one box makes that box twice as wide as a box in a row of two — left alone, a 24%
share in the wide box would draw the same length as a 48% share in a narrow one.
Scaling puts every bar on one scale, so equal lengths mean equal shares wherever
they sit.

### The one move

The one move is computed by `computeMapMove()` from the `mapMove` frontmatter
block:

- `reclaimPriority` — question ids in priority order; the reclaim target is the
  first eligible one.
- `redirectPriority` — same, for the redirect target (the two never collide).
- **An answer is eligible for a half of the move only if it supplies that half's
  sentence** (`reclaimSentence` / `redirectSentence`). Requiring it is what stops
  the walk dying on a high-priority answer that has no copy for this half: before
  the rule applied to `slipping` answers too, `scrum-master-ai`'s "status and
  logistics desk" (first in `redirectPriority`, with a `reclaimSentence` but no
  `redirectSentence`) won the redirect on 16% of answer sets and then rendered
  nothing, so takers were told what to stop doing and never told where the time
  should go.
- **That also lets a `context` answer win either half.** "Not your fault" is not
  the same as "not important": some constraints are real problems the taker can't
  ignore, and leaving those in the soft context strip understates them. Writing
  the sentence is the opt-in — an author who writes one has decided this
  constraint is actionable — and it promotes the answer to the move, so the
  problem lands in the most prominent block on the page while still being named
  without blame in the map. It stays out of the slipping column either way.
- If nothing is slipping, the map renders the `wellPositioned` fallback instead
  of a move, unless a context answer won either half of it: the fallback replaces
  the move, so it would otherwise swallow the problem just surfaced.
- `framing` (optional `{ gaining, mixed, slipping }`) classifies the result from
  the ratio of gaining to slipping answers (context/mixed ignored). The results
  page does not print it: it exists so `levelTagPrefix` has a tier to tag with.
  Omit it and no result-tier tag is applied.

The `mapMove` block also holds the surrounding copy (`eyebrow`, `heading`,
`opening`, `shape`, column headings, `close`, `cta`, …) so the engine
stays free of site-specific wording. The `cta` is a footer row: one line of
secondary text (`body`) plus one accent link (`buttonLabel` / `buttonHref`). The
map-move results page renders the `MapMoveResults.astro` component directly from
frontmatter, not from the MDX body (which stays empty for these quizzes).

Query shape: `map-move` encodes the raw answers as a single `a` param

## 2026-08-05 — Quiz copy acted on the 29 July feedback session

**Why.** Mark walked the quiz through a live critique on 29 July. Most of it was
acted on within a day (email capture back at the end, the role question, the
question copy pass), but six items were still outstanding a week later. This is
those six.

**The results heading was the largest one.** `heading: 'Here's what I see'` was
the H1 on the results page and said nothing about the person reading it, while
the sentence that *did* ("Most of your last few Sprints went to the mechanical
work") sat two blocks below as the shape's `mostLine`. The specific sentence was
in the wrong place, so it swapped up into the heading: `mapMove.heading` now takes
the same `{box}` substitution `mostLine` already had, and `scrum-master-ai` drops
`mostLine` rather than printing the same sentence twice. The first thing on the
page is now about the taker instead of about the page. `mostlyTop` / `mostlyBottom`
stay as the reading line under the shape, still suppressed when the largest box
already sits on the majority row. `headingFallback` covers the case where the
heading wants a `{box}` and no shape was computed; for this quiz that needs every
answered option to lack a `box`, so it is a guard rather than a path anyone hits.

**"About your situation" is now "the constraints you described".** Naming what
the strip actually contains rather than gesturing at it. One option sits oddly
under that heading, q8's "I coach through the work as I go", which is a
legitimate way to work and not a constraint; that is one option in thirty-two and
was accepted rather than reworded.

**The page now points forward at the payoff.** The critique was that the single
most valuable block sits last with nothing above leading up to it. Two changes,
no reorder: `opening` ends by saying what is coming ("Below: where your Sprints
actually went, then the one change I'd make first"), and the shape's move tags
went from `less of this` / `more of this` to `take time from here` / `put it
here`, which is the same language the move block itself uses. Worth knowing that
the long tag can only ever land on the mechanical box: `reclaimPriority` is
q3/q1/q2 and every eligible answer in those three is `box: mechanical`, which is
the full-width bottom row. The short tag is the one that lands on a half-width
top-row box.

**Three question stems were still too long** (q5 at 146 characters, q7 at 190, q8
at 140). The 30 July copy pass fixed tone, not length. Trimming these is safe for
the reason recorded in that entry: question and answer text are read together, so
a phrase in the stem that the options already carry is dead weight, which is the
opposite of the rule for result sentences. q5 lost the list its options already
name, q7 kept a shortened list because "better at their own job" is undefined
without one, and q8 lost "the way they work together", which overlapped q4.

**"Get one thing to try" became "focus on".** "Try" reads as "maybe this will
work, maybe it won't", which undersells the one block the whole page is built
around.

**Two defects fixed in passing:** `close` read "GenAI will not magically you or
your team more productive", and `slippingEmpty` had no full stop.

**Still outstanding from the same session, deliberately.** Role-conditional
result copy (the role tag reaches Cakemail and drives the manager `lens`, but
nothing on the results page varies by it) and a pain-led hero kicker. Both need
copy only Mark can write, and the role one needs a decision about how far to take
it: the critique proposed roles × result buckets, which is a 4× multiplier on
copy maintained by one person.

1 # Astro Quiz Engine 2 3 A small, self-contained quiz engine for Astro sites. Quiz content lives in MDX 4 files under a content collection; the engine provides the schema, the scoring 5 helpers, a React stepper component, and a results-page primitive. 6 7 The engine is intentionally generic. It has no opinion about: 8 9 - where the user lands afterward (you provide the `onSubmit` callback) 10 - where leads go (CRM, email tool, JSON file, whatever) 11 - what the level labels mean ("high-risk", "tier-1", "beach" -- all opaque 12 strings to the engine) 13 - styling beyond Tailwind utility classes 14 15 ## Quick start 16 17 ### 1. Register the content collection 18 19 ```ts 20 // src/content.config.ts 21 import { defineCollection } from 'astro:content'; 22 import { glob } from 'astro/loaders'; 23 import { createQuizSchema } from '@/lib/quiz-engine'; 24 25 const quizzes = defineCollection({ 26 loader: glob({ pattern: '**/*.mdx', base: './src/content/quizzes' }), 27 schema: (ctx) => createQuizSchema(ctx), 28 }); 29 30 export const collections = { quizzes /* + your others */ }; 31 ``` 32 33 `createQuizSchema` follows the [`SchemaContext`](https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/modules/astro-content/) pattern used by Starlight and recommended in the Astro docs: it receives the schema context (which carries Astro's `image()` helper) so section images can be content-relative paths that get optimized through Astro's asset pipeline. The returned Zod object can be `.extend()`ed with site-specific frontmatter fields: 34 35 ```ts 36 schema: (ctx) => 37 createQuizSchema(ctx).extend({ 38 heroHeading: z.string().optional(), 39 }), 40 ``` 41 42 ### 2. Author a quiz in MDX 43 44 ```mdx 45 --- 46 title: 'How GenAI Fails in Software Teams' 47 intro: 'Twelve questions. Three minutes.' 48 sections: 49 - id: delivery 50 label: 'Delivery & Outcomes' 51 blurb: 'What happens when AI code reaches production.' 52 questions: 53 - id: q1 54 section: delivery 55 text: 'In the METR study, senior devs using AI on familiar code were:' 56 reveal: 'Self-reported productivity is unreliable.' 57 options: 58 - { text: '20% faster', score: 0 } 59 - { text: 'about the same', score: 0 } 60 - { text: '19% slower', score: 1 } 61 - { text: '50% slower', score: 0 } 62 sectionLevels: 63 - { level: 'high-risk', minScore: 0, maxScore: 0 } 64 - { level: 'low-risk', minScore: 1, maxScore: 1 } 65 overallLevels: 66 - { level: 'high-risk', minScore: 0, maxScore: 0, title: 'High Risk' } 67 - { level: 'low-risk', minScore: 1, maxScore: 1, title: 'Low Risk' } 68 randomize: within-sections # optional; defaults to 'none' 69 --- 70 71 import ResultCard from '@/lib/quiz-engine/components/ResultCard.astro'; 72 73 74 ### Delivery & Outcomes You haven't seen the METR study yet. 75 76 77 78 ### Delivery & Outcomes You already know perceived productivity outruns real 79 productivity. 80 81 ``` 82 83 ### 3. Render the stepper on a landing page 84 85 ```astro 86 --- 87 // src/pages/quiz/[slug].astro 88 import { getEntry } from 'astro:content'; 89 import QuizStepper from '@/lib/quiz-engine/components/QuizStepper'; 90 91 const entry = await getEntry('quizzes', Astro.params.slug); 92 if (!entry) return Astro.redirect('/404'); 93 --- 94 95 101 ``` 102 103 Scoring happens in the browser via `computeQuizResult` + `buildResultQuery` from 104 the engine. On submit, the stepper assembles `email`, `custom_attributes[firstname]`, 105 and any tags as multipart form-data, delivers them (see below), then redirects to 106 `/quiz/{slug}/results/?...` with the locally-computed query string. 107 108 **Delivery is pluggable. Provide EITHER:** 109 110 - `cakemailFormUrl?: string` — built-in path. POSTs the form-data straight to a 111 Cakemail hosted-form action URL with `mode: 'no-cors'` (fire-and-forget). This 112 is best-effort: a network error is logged but the user still reaches their 113 results. Good for a simple standalone setup. 114 - `onSubmit?: (formData: FormData) => Promise` — host owns delivery. Receives 115 the assembled form-data; route it through your own endpoint (e.g. a CAPTCHA-gated 116 proxy, or any ESP). Unlike the built-in path this hook is **authoritative**: if it 117 throws, the engine shows the thrown message and keeps the user on the capture step 118 to retry; resolve to proceed to results. If both are supplied, `onSubmit` wins. 119 120 To mount a widget the host needs at submit time (e.g. a CAPTCHA whose token your 121 `onSubmit` reads), pass it via: 122 123 - `captureExtras?: React.ReactNode` — rendered inside the capture form, just above 124 the submit button. Opaque to the engine. 125 126 > APR uses these to gate the quiz behind Cloudflare Turnstile: a wrapper supplies 127 > `captureExtras={}` and an `onSubmit` that appends the token and POSTs 128 > to a server endpoint, keeping this engine free of Turnstile/ESP specifics. 129 130 Two optional props drive audience tagging, sent as Cakemail's `tags[]=true` 131 form fields alongside the email: 132 133 - `submissionTags?: string[]` — static tags applied to every submission (e.g. 134 `['aiquiz']`). Use these as the segment an ESP automation triggers on. 135 - `levelTagPrefix?: string` — when set, also tags `${levelTagPrefix}${overallLevel}` 136 (e.g. `'aiquiz-'` + a computed level `'high-risk'` => `aiquiz-high-risk`), so a 137 nurture sequence can branch on the result tier. 138 139 Note: the tag field names follow Cakemail's hosted-form convention. With `onSubmit` 140 you can remap them to any ESP before sending. 141 142 Capture copy is overridable so it can read correctly wherever the step sits: 143 `captureHeading`, `captureBody`, `captureButtonLabel` (the capture form's own 144 button) and `captureFootnote`. `submitButtonLabel` is a separate prop: it labels 145 whichever button _finishes_ the quiz and goes to the results. 146 147 Keep those two straight. On a start gate the capture button leads to question 1, 148 so it defaults to `startButtonLabel`; a finish label there ("See my results") 149 promises something the next screen doesn't deliver. 150 151 ### 4. Render the results 152 153 ```astro 154 --- 155 // src/pages/quiz/[slug]/results.astro 156 export const prerender = false; 157 import { getEntry, render } from 'astro:content'; 158 159 const entry = await getEntry('quizzes', Astro.params.slug); 160 if (!entry) return Astro.redirect('/404'); 161 const { Content } = await render(entry); 162 --- 163 164

Your results

165

166 Score: {Astro.url.searchParams.get('total')} / { 167 Astro.url.searchParams.get('max') 168 } 169

170 171 172 ``` 173 174 The `` blocks inside the MDX body check the URL search params and 175 render only when the requested section/level matches. 176 177 `` takes `section` and `level` (both required) plus an optional 178 `image`. Pass an imported `ImageMetadata` (preferred, so Astro optimizes it) or 179 a plain URL string to show a small icon atop the card. A common pattern is to 180 reuse the same per-section icons from the landing page so the results mirror it: 181 182 ```mdx 183 import ResultCard from '@/lib/quiz-engine/components/ResultCard.astro'; 184 import deliveryIcon from './images/delivery.png'; 185 186 187 ### Delivery & Outcomes You haven't seen the METR study yet. 188 189 ``` 190 191 ## Public API 192 193 ```ts 194 import { 195 // schema 196 createQuizSchema, 197 198 // pure scoring 199 computeQuizResult, 200 buildResultQuery, 201 findLevel, 202 getOptionScore, 203 getMaxQuestionScore, 204 205 // true for questions that count toward the score, map and progress 206 isScored, 207 208 // types 209 type QuizData, ... 3	A short, human-readable log of notable changes and the reasoning behind them.
4	Newest first. (Detailed, current behaviour lives in `CLAUDE.md`; this file is the
5	"why we did it" story.)
